questions.def: "Enough" means sufficient quantity and is used with uncountable nouns.
questions.question: I don't have ___ money to buy a new car.

questions.def: "Most" refers to the majority without specifying a particular group.
questions.question: ___ of the students passed the exam.

questions.def: "Little" is used with uncountable nouns like milk.
questions.question: There is very ___ milk left in the fridge.

questions.def: "Few" means not many and is used with countable nouns.
questions.question: ___ people know the answer to this question.

questions.def: "Several" means more than two but not many.
questions.question: I have read ___ books on this topic.

questions.def: "Other" is used to refer to an alternative.
questions.question: I have no ___ choice but to agree.

questions.def: "A lot of" is used with both countable and uncountable nouns.
questions.question: He has ___ experience in this field.

questions.def: "Every piece" refers to each individual part of the cake.
questions.question: ___ of the cake was delicious.

questions.def: "Both" is used to refer to two people or things.
questions.question: ___ my parents are teachers.

questions.def: "More" indicates a greater quantity of uncountable time.
questions.question: I need ___ time to finish this project.

questions.def: "Each" emphasizes individuality within a group.
questions.question: ___ student is responsible for their own work.

questions.def: "Every" shouldn't be followed by "of". Use "Every one of the books".
questions.question: Every of the books are very interesting.

questions.def: "Whole" refers to the complete pizza.
questions.question: I ate the ___ pizza by myself.

questions.def: "All" refers to the entire quantity of juice.
questions.question: He drank ___ of the juice.

questions.def: "Most of us" refers to a majority of the group.
questions.question: ___ of us enjoyed the party.

questions.def: "Much" is for uncountable nouns; use "Many" for people.
questions.question: Much people came to the party.

questions.def: "Several" indicates more than two but not many.
questions.question: I have visited ___ countries in Europe.

questions.def: "Little" means almost no time (uncountable).
questions.question: I have ___ time to help you today.

questions.def: "Some of" indicates a portion of the group.
questions.question: ___ the students are from different countries.

questions.def: Should be "A lot of people" or "Many people".
questions.question: A lot people enjoy watching movies online.

questions.def: "Enough" means a sufficient amount.
questions.question: Do you have ___ sugar for the cake?

questions.def: "Some" refers to a portion of uncountable information.
questions.question: ___ of the information was useful.

questions.def: "A few" means a small number and is used with countable nouns.
questions.question: ___ of the books are missing.

questions.def: "Each" refers to individuals in a group separately.
questions.question: ___ person needs to bring their ID.

questions.def: "Much" is used with uncountable nouns in negative sentences.
questions.question: There isn't ___ milk in the fridge.

questions.def: "Several" means more than two but not many (countable).
questions.question: ___ of the apples were rotten.

questions.def: Use 'some' for affirmative statements when referring to an unspecified quantity.
questions.question: I need ___ information about the job.

questions.def: 'Enough' means sufficient quantity, suitable in this context.
questions.question: Do you have ___ money for the bus?

questions.def: 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns like 'time'.
questions.question: I don't have ___ time to finish this task.

questions.def: 'Fewer' is used with countable nouns like 'people'.
questions.question: ___ people came to the party than expected.
